extracted.intended_audience: news consumers, journalism educators, and news organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Trust Project's 8 Trust Indicators to evaluate whether a news story or news organization is trustworthy, by checking expertise, purpose, sourcing, local knowledge, diversity, feedback mechanisms, reporting methods, and organizational best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise: The journalist is an expert
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist should base what they say on solid evidence, careful reporting and strict standards; readers rely on journalists to provide accurate information about events they rarely witness themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Who made this? Do they have a good professional reputation? Are they reporting on an area they normally focus on? (Look for demonstrated expertise, relevant beats, and a record of reliable reporting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels: The purpose of the story is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose — why this was written — should be clear so readers can judge bias. Distinguish advertising/sponsored content (meant to persuade) from journalism (meant to help readers form their own opinions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Why has this been created? Does this have a clear opinion, or is it impartial? Is this sponsored, or is it advertising something? Is the purpose clearly indicated? (Check for clear labeling of opinion, ads, sponsored content.)

rubrics_metrics.name: References: You can find and access the sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources are where journalists get information (eyewitness accounts, official reports, etc.). When sources are shown, readers can verify reliability and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: What’s the source? For investigative, in-depth, or controversial stories, do we have access to the sources behind the claims? Can you find another source to back up what is being said? (Look for named sources, links, documents, and transparency about source types.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Local: The journalist uses local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalist who knows and lives in the community can explain events more accurately; being on the scene and speaking to those present yields up-to-date and context-rich reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Was the reporting done with deep knowledge about the local situation or community? Was the journalist on the scene? Does the story let you know when the news sources are local? (Check for indicators of local presence and context.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity: The story brings in many kinds of people
rubrics_metrics.description: News should include a range of voices and experiences (race, class, generation, gender, sexual orientation, region) so readers get a fuller picture and groups aren’t stereotyped or omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: What are the newsroom’s efforts and commitments to bring in diverse perspectives? Are some communities included only in stereotypical ways, or even completely missing? (Assess sourcing breadth and representation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable Feedback: The news organization allows readers to participate
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting and listening to public feedback helps journalists correct errors, update incomplete stories, and discover important reporting leads; public participation can improve accuracy and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Can we participate? Can we give feedback? Does the news site invite and acknowledge contributions from the public? (Look for comment systems, correction forms, reader surveys, contact channels, and evidence of responsiveness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: We can tell the process used to make the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining why a story was chosen and how it was researched helps readers understand how the reporting came together and indicates the story’s depth, rigor, and balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: How was it made? How long did it take to make? Who else was involved in the process? (Look for methodology notes, reporting timelines, named contributors, and description of research techniques.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practices: The journalist or news organization explains their ownership and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations that publish rules or standards (fact-checking, corrections policy, funding disclosure, mission) are more trustworthy; absence of standards or secretive ownership can reduce trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Does the journalist or organization have a list of rules that they have to follow? How do they check their facts? Who funds them? What is the organization’s mission and priorities? Does the journalist or organization make corrections if they are wrong? Do they have a commitment to ethical/diverse/accurate reporting and how do they show they are sticking to the rules? (Look for transparency pages, corrections logs, funding disclosures, and stated editorial policies.)
